title: Building a Python Framework to Monitor IDMC Taskflow Execution
author: Shireesha Mangannagari
summary: Starting an Informatica Intelligent Data Management Cloud (IDMC) taskflow from code is easy. Knowing what happened to it afterward is harder. In most pipelines I've reviewed, the "monitoring" is a scheduled job that fires the taskflow and hopes for the best. When a run hangs, gets suspended, or quietly fails at 2 a.m., nobody finds out until a downstream report is empty. This post walks through a small Python framework that fixes that. It: Authenticates to IDMC and renews the session when it expires Starts a taskflow and captures its run ID Polls run status with exponential backoff and a hard timeout Treats FAILED, SUSPENDED, and timeouts as distinct outcomes Sends alerts through pluggable notifiers (Slack, Amazon SNS, or anything else) Emits structured JSON logs you can query in CloudWatch, Datadog, or Splunk All of it fits in about 300 lines and works the same on a laptop, in a container, or inside AWS Lambda. Note: IDMC endpoint paths and status values can vary by pod and release. The ones below match the public REST API docs at the time of writing. Check them against your org's API reference before going to production. The architecture The framework has four parts: Step 1: Configuration Keep credentials out of code. A small dataclass reads them from environment variables, and in AWS those can come from Secrets Manager. # idmc_monitor/config.py import os from dataclasses import dataclass , field @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class IDMCConfig : username : str password : str login_url : str = "https://dm-us.informaticacloud.com/saas/public/core/v3/login" poll_initial_seconds : float = 10.0 poll_max_seconds : float = 120.0 timeout_seconds : float = 3600.0 request_timeout : float = 30.0 terminal_failure_states : frozenset = field ( default_factory = lambda : frozenset ( { "FAILED" , "SUSPENDED" , "FAULTED" , "ABORTED" } ) ) terminal_success_states : frozenset = field ( default_factory = lambda : frozenset ( { "SUCCESS" , "COMPLETED" } ) ) @classmethod def from_env ( cls ) -> "IDMCConfig" : return cls ( username = os . environ [ "IDMC_USERNAME" ] , password = os . environ [ "IDMC_PASSWORD" ] , login_url = os . environ . get ( "IDMC_LOGIN_URL" , cls . login_url ) , timeout_seconds = float ( os . environ . get ( "IDMC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS" , 3600 ) ) , ) The login URL depends on your region (dm-us, dm-em, dm-ap, and so on), so it's configurable. Step 2: A session that renews itself An IDMC session times out after a period of inactivity. Long-running taskflows can outlast it, so the client has to notice a 401 and log in again without failing the run. The v3 login response returns a sessionId and a baseApiUrl for your pod. Application Integration endpoints (/active-bpel/...) live on the same pod host, without the /saas suffix. # idmc_monitor/session.py import logging from urllib . parse import urlparse import requests from requests . adapters import HTTPAdapter from urllib3 . util . retry import Retry from . config import IDMCConfig log = logging . getLogger ( __name__ ) class IDMCAuthError ( RuntimeError ) : pass class IDMCSession : """Wraps requests.Session with IDMC login and automatic re-login.""" def __init__ ( self , config : IDMCConfig ) : self . config = config self . _http = requests . Session ( ) retry = Retry ( total = 5 , backoff_factor = 1.5 , status_forcelist = ( 429 , 500 , 502 , 503 , 504 ) , allowed_methods = frozenset ( { "GET" , "POST" } ) , ) self . _http . mount ( "https://" , HTTPAdapter ( max_retries = retry ) ) self . session_id : str | None = None self . base_api_url : str | None = None self . pod_url : str | None = None def login ( self ) -> None : resp = self . _http . post ( self . config . login_url , json = { "username" : self . config . username , "password" : self . config . password } , timeout = self . config . request_timeout , ) if resp . status_code != 200 : raise IDMCAuthError ( f "Login failed: HTTP {resp.status_code}" ) body = resp . json ( ) self . session_id = body [ "userInfo" ] [ "sessionId" ] self . base_api_url = body [ "products" ] [ 0 ] [ "baseApiUrl" ] parsed = urlparse ( self . base_api_url ) self . pod_url = f "{parsed.scheme}://{parsed.netloc}" log . info ( "idmc_login_ok" , extra = { "pod" : self . pod_url } ) def request ( self , method : str , url : str , ** kwargs ) -> requests . Response : if not self . session_id : self . login ( ) for attempt in ( 1 , 2 ) : headers = kwargs . pop ( "headers" , { } ) | { "INFA-SESSION-ID" : self . session_id , "icSessionId" : self . session_id , "Accept" : "application/json" , } resp = self . _http . request ( method , url , headers = headers , timeout = self . config . request_timeout , ** kwargs , ) if resp . status_code == 401 and attempt == 1 : log . warning ( "idmc_session_expired_relogin" ) self . login ( ) continue resp . raise_for_status ( ) return resp raise IDMCAuthError ( "Request still unauthorized after re-login" ) Two layers of resilience run here. urllib3.Retry handles transient network errors and 5xx/429 responses. The explicit 401 branch handles session expiry, which a generic retry can't fix. Step 3: The monitor This is the core of the framework. It starts the taskflow, then polls until one of three things happens: success, failure, or timeout. # idmc_monitor/monitor.py import logging import random import time from dataclasses import dataclass , field from enum import Enum from . config import IDMCConfig from . notifiers import Notifier from . session import IDMCSession log = logging . getLogger ( __name__ ) class Outcome ( str , Enum ) : SUCCESS = "SUCCESS" FAILED = "FAILED" TIMEOUT = "TIMEOUT" @dataclass class RunResult : taskflow : str run_id : str outcome : Outcome final_status : str duration_seconds : float details : dict = field ( default_factory = dict ) class TaskflowMonitor : def __init__ ( self , session : IDMCSession , config : IDMCConfig , notifiers : list [ Notifier ] | None = None ) : self . session = session self . config = config self . notifiers = notifiers or [ ] # -- API calls ----------------------------------------------------- def start ( self , taskflow : str , params : dict | None = None ) -> str : if not self . session . pod_url : self . session . login ( ) url = f "{self.session.pod_url}/active-bpel/rt/{taskflow}" resp = self . session . request ( "POST" , url , json = params or { } ) run_id = str ( resp . json ( ) [ "RunId" ] ) log . info ( "taskflow_started" , extra = { "taskflow" : taskflow , "run_id" : run_id } ) return run_id def get_status ( self , run_id : str ) -> dict : url = f "{self.session.pod_url}/active-bpel/services/tf/status/{run_id}" return self . session . request ( "GET" , url ) . json ( ) # -- Polling loop -------------------------------------------------- def _next_delay ( self , current : float ) -> float : """Exponential backoff with full jitter, capped at poll_max_seconds.""" grown = min ( current * 2 , self . config . poll_max_seconds ) return random . uniform ( self . config . poll_initial_seconds , grown ) def wait ( self , taskflow : str , run_id : str ) -> RunResult : started = time . monotonic ( ) delay = self . config . poll_initial_seconds last_status = "UNKNOWN" payload : dict = { } while True : elapsed = time . monotonic ( ) - started if elapsed > self . config . timeout_seconds : return self . _finish ( taskflow , run_id , Outcome . TIMEOUT , last_status , elapsed , payload ) payload = self . get_status ( run_id ) last_status = str ( payload . get ( "status" , "UNKNOWN" ) ) . upper ( ) log . info ( "taskflow_status" , extra = { "taskflow" : taskflow , "run_id" : run_id , "status" : last_status , "elapsed" : round ( elapsed , 1 ) , } ) if last_status in self . config . terminal_success_states : return self . _finish ( taskflow , run_id , Outcome . SUCCESS , last_status , elapsed , payload ) if last_status in self . config . terminal_failure_states : return self . _finish ( taskflow , run_id , Outcome . FAILED , last_status , elapsed , payload ) time . sleep ( delay ) delay = self . _next_delay ( delay ) def run ( self , taskflow : str , params : dict | None = None ) -> RunResult : run_id = self . start ( taskflow , params ) return self . wait ( taskflow , run_id ) # -- Outcome handling ---------------------------------------------- def _finish ( self , taskflow , run_id , outcome , status , elapsed , payload ) -> RunResult : result = RunResult ( taskflow , run_id , outcome , status , round ( elapsed , 1 ) , payload ) log . info ( "taskflow_finished" , extra = { "taskflow" : taskflow , "run_id" : run_id , "outcome" : outcome . value , "status" : status , "duration_seconds" : result . duration_seconds , } ) if outcome is not Outcome . SUCCESS : for notifier in self . notifiers : try : notifier . send ( result ) except Exception : # an alert failure must never mask the run result log . exception ( "notifier_failed" , extra = { "notifier" : type ( notifier ) . __name__ } ) return result A few design choices are worth explaining. Why jittered backoff? If you run 40 taskflows at once and they all poll every 10 seconds, they hit the API in lockstep. Jitter spreads the calls out and keeps you clear of rate limits. The cap at poll_max_seconds keeps a long run from going unchecked for too long. Why is TIMEOUT its own outcome? A timeout doesn't mean the taskflow failed. It may still be running. Keeping it separate lets on-call engineers decide whether to wait, cancel, or escalate, instead of treating every timeout as a failure. Why catch notifier exceptions? If Slack is down, you still want the correct RunResult returned and logged. Alerting is best-effort. The run result is the source of truth. Step 4: Pluggable notifiers Each channel implements one method. Adding Teams, PagerDuty, or email means adding one small class. # idmc_monitor/notifiers.py import json from typing import Protocol import requests class Notifier ( Protocol ) : def send ( self , result ) -> None : . . . def _summary ( result ) -> str : return ( f "IDMC taskflow *{result.taskflow}* ended as *{result.outcome.value}* " f "(status={result.final_status}, run_id={result.run_id}, " f "{result.duration_seconds}s)" ) class SlackNotifier : def __init__ ( self , webhook_url : str ) : self . webhook_url = webhook_url def send ( self , result ) -> None : requests . post ( self . webhook_url , json = { "text" : _summary ( result ) } , timeout = 10 ) class SNSNotifier : def __init__ ( self , topic_arn : str , client = None ) : import boto3 self . topic_arn = topic_arn self . client = client or boto3 . client ( "sns" ) def send ( self , result ) -> None : self . client . publish ( TopicArn = self . topic_arn , Subject = f "IDMC {result.outcome.value}: {result.taskflow}" [ : 100 ] , Message = json . dumps ( { "taskflow" : result . taskflow , "run_id" : result . run_id , "outcome" : result . outcome . value , "status" : result . final_status , "duration_seconds" : result . duration_seconds , } ) , ) SNS fans out to email, SMS, Lambda, or an SQS queue, so one notifier covers a lot of ground in AWS. Step 5: Structured logs Plain-text logs are hard to query. A short JSON formatter turns every extra={...} field into a searchable key. # idmc_monitor/logging_setup.py import json import logging _STANDARD = set ( vars ( logging . makeLogRecord ( { } ) ) ) class JsonFormatter ( logging . Formatter ) : def format ( self , record : logging . LogRecord ) -> str : data = { "level" : record . levelname , "event" : record . getMessage ( ) , "logger" : record . name , "ts" : self . formatTime ( record ) } data . update ( { k : v for k , v in vars ( record ) . items ( ) if k not in _STANDARD } ) return json . dumps ( data , default = str ) def configure ( level : int = logging . INFO ) -> None : handler = logging . StreamHandler ( ) handler . setFormatter ( JsonFormatter ( ) ) logging . basicConfig ( level = level , handlers = [ handler ] , force = True ) Now a CloudWatch Logs Insights query like this works out of the box: fields ts, taskflow, outcome, duration_seconds | filter event = "taskflow_finished" | stats avg(duration_seconds), count(*) by taskflow, outcome That one query gives you average run time and failure counts for each taskflow. Step 6: A CLI entry point # idmc_monitor/cli.py import argparse import json import os import sys from . config import IDMCConfig from . logging_setup import configure from . monitor import Outcome , TaskflowMonitor from . notifiers import SlackNotifier from . session import IDMCSession def main ( ) -> int : parser = argparse . ArgumentParser ( description = "Run and monitor an IDMC taskflow" ) parser . add_argument ( "taskflow" , help = "Published taskflow API name" ) parser . add_argument ( "--params" , default = "{}" , help = "JSON input parameters" ) args = parser . parse_args ( ) configure ( ) config = IDMCConfig . from_env ( ) notifiers = [ ] if hook := os . environ . get ( "SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL" ) : notifiers . append ( SlackNotifier ( hook ) ) monitor = TaskflowMonitor ( IDMCSession ( config ) , config , notifiers ) result = monitor . run ( args . taskflow , json . loads ( args . params ) ) exit_codes = { Outcome . SUCCESS : 0 , Outcome . FAILED : 1 , Outcome . TIMEOUT : 2 } return exit_codes [ result . outcome ] if __name__ == "__main__" : sys . exit ( main ( ) ) Different exit codes for failure and timeout let schedulers like Airflow, Control-M, or a CI pipeline react to each one differently. export IDMC_USERNAME = svc_integration export IDMC_PASSWORD = '********' python -m idmc_monitor.cli tf_daily_gl_load --params '{"run_date": "2026-11-10"}' Step 7: Test it without touching IDMC Because the session is injected, you can swap it for a fake and test the polling logic in milliseconds. # tests/test_monitor.py from unittest . mock import MagicMock , patch from idmc_monitor . config import IDMCConfig from idmc_monitor . monitor import Outcome , TaskflowMonitor def make_monitor ( statuses , notifier = None , timeout = 60 ) : cfg = IDMCConfig ( username = "u" , password = "p" , poll_initial_seconds = 0.01 , poll_max_seconds = 0.02 , timeout_seconds = timeout ) session = MagicMock ( pod_url = "https://pod.example.com" ) responses = iter ( statuses ) session . request . side_effect = lambda m , url , ** kw : MagicMock ( json = lambda : { "RunId" : "42" } if m == "POST" else { "status" : next ( responses ) } ) return TaskflowMonitor ( session , cfg , [ notifier ] if notifier else [ ] ) @patch ( "time.sleep" , return_value = None ) def test_success_after_running ( _ ) : result = make_monitor ( [ "RUNNING" , "RUNNING" , "SUCCESS" ] ) . run ( "tf_demo" ) assert result . outcome is Outcome . SUCCESS assert result . run_id == "42" @patch ( "time.sleep" , return_value = None ) def test_failure_triggers_notifier ( _ ) : notifier = MagicMock ( ) result = make_monitor ( [ "RUNNING" , "FAILED" ] , notifier ) . run ( "tf_demo" ) assert result . outcome is Outcome . FAILED notifier . send . assert_called_once ( ) @patch ( "time.sleep" , return_value = None ) def test_notifier_error_does_not_mask_result ( _ ) : notifier = MagicMock ( ) notifier . send . side_effect = RuntimeError ( "slack down" ) result = make_monitor ( [ "SUSPENDED" ] , notifier ) . run ( "tf_demo" ) assert result . outcome is Outcome . FAILED Run them with pytest -q. A timeout test works the same way: set timeout_seconds=0 and feed it endless RUNNING statuses. Running it on AWS The framework has no AWS dependency at its core, so you can choose where it runs: AWS Lambda: Good for taskflows that finish within the 15-minute Lambda limit. Package the module as a Lambda layer and call monitor.run() from the handler. AWS Step Functions: Better for long runs. Use one Lambda to call start() and another to call get_status() once. Then let a Step Functions Wait + Choice loop do the polling. You pay nothing while waiting, and there's no timeout ceiling. ECS Fargate or a scheduler container: Good when the monitor is one step in a bigger batch job. For Step Functions, split the monitor like this: def start_handler ( event , _ctx ) : run_id = monitor . start ( event [ "taskflow" ] , event . get ( "params" ) ) return { ** event , "run_id" : run_id } def status_handler ( event , _ctx ) : status = str ( monitor . get_status ( event [ "run_id" ] ) . get ( "status" , "" ) ) . upper ( ) return { ** event , "status" : status } The state machine checks status and either loops back through a Wait state or branches to success or failure. Production checklist Before you rely on this in production: ☐ Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, never in environment files committed to Git. ☐ Use a dedicated IDMC service account with only the permissions the taskflows need. ☐ Confirm the status values your pod returns and adjust terminal_*_states to match. ☐ Set timeout_seconds per taskflow based on historical run times. A 95th-percentile duration plus a buffer works well. ☐ Add a CloudWatch alarm on the taskflow_finished metric filter for outcome != SUCCESS, as a backstop in case a notifier fails. ☐ Make your taskflows idempotent so a retry after a timeout doesn't double-load data. Wrapping up Starting a taskflow is one API call. Trusting it in production takes a bit more: a session that renews itself, polling that respects rate limits, clear outcomes, and alerts that can't hide the real result. With this framework, every IDMC run either reports success or tells someone exactly what went wrong, with the run ID, the final status, and how long it took. What's next: In a follow-up post, I'll pull IDMC activity-log data into a dashboard so you can see run-time trends and failure hotspots across every taskflow in your org. If you're running IDMC at scale, I'd like to hear how you handle monitoring today. Share your approach in the comments.

title: Why does my PyTorch DataLoader fail when a worker touches CUDA?
author: CloudGPU
summary: I work on CloudGPU. Keep dataset decoding and collation on the CPU, then move each batch to CUDA in the main training process. If a worker initializes CUDA after a fork, adding more workers can expose a process-initialization problem rather than a model problem. 1. Find the CUDA operation inside the worker Inspect Dataset.__getitem__ , transforms, collate_fn and worker_init_fn . Remove .cuda() , .to("cuda") and accelerator model construction from those paths. Also check whether a tensor was created on CUDA when the dataset object was built. Use num_workers=0 temporarily to obtain a clearer traceback. It is a diagnostic step, not a recommendation about throughput. 2. Give the loader CPU data and an explicit process context Save this as loader_boundary.py in an environment with a suitable PyTorch CUDA build: import torch from torch . utils . data import DataLoader , Dataset class Samples ( Dataset ) : def __len__ ( self ) : return 12 def __getitem__ ( self , index ) : return torch . tensor ( [ index ] , dtype = torch . float32 ) def main ( ) : if not torch . cuda . is_available ( ) : raise RuntimeError ( "CUDA is not available in this environment" ) loader = DataLoader ( Samples ( ) , batch_size = 3 , num_workers = 2 , multiprocessing_context = "spawn" , pin_memory = True , ) for cpu_batch in loader : assert cpu_batch . device . type == "cpu" gpu_batch = cpu_batch . to ( "cuda" , non_blocking = True ) assert gpu_batch . device . type == "cuda" if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) python3 loader_boundary.py Keep the dataset class at module scope and the execution behind the main guard. Run the example as a script, rather than assuming an interactive notebook can spawn the same definitions. CPU-only workers still need review for picklable objects and import-time side effects. 3. Restore your real data pipeline one part at a time Add the real decoder first, then transforms, then collation. Keep the device transfer in the main loop. This isolates the first change that reintroduces CUDA into a worker. This answer does not diagnose every worker crash: unreadable inputs and CPU resource exhaustion need separate investigation. The official DataLoader documentation recommends CPU batches and memory pinning instead of returning CUDA tensors from multiprocess loading. The multiprocessing guidance explains accelerator initialization and process start methods. For rental-side execution boundaries, see the CloudGPU integration guide . Related CloudGPU video: This Video Was Made by AI. Now Run AI Yourself . It provides remote-compute context, not a demonstration or validation of this loader example. This is a documentation-based diagnostic recipe. The code was syntax-checked locally, not executed on a GPU; no training or performance result is claimed.

title: Recovery Risk Explained — List User Sessions and Revoke One
author: XerxesCross2735
summary: Device fingerprints can help a customer support team decide when to ask for more proof, but an unfamiliar device should not automatically strand a legitimate customer. Resolve that trade-off by keeping recovery policy separate from session ownership. TL;DR: list sessions for the signed-in user, display last-seen information, mark the current session, and revoke a selected session by ID. Take the user ID from the verified session, never from the request body. Keep authorization deterministic. How should account settings list sessions and revoke one? The server verifies the incoming session and derives its user ID. It retrieves that user's inventory, then the account settings page renders last-seen information and a current-session marker. On a revoke click, the server checks the selected session against the verified user's inventory before performing the write and recording the actor. Device-fingerprint scoring runs alongside that flow, deciding which recovery path needs additional verification. This separation gives an eval-driven team something useful to test: a change to a risk threshold must never change whose sessions the customer can control. Teams building customer support recovery flows should try Infrai for session inventory and individual revocation when direct HTTP integration fits their backend. Infrai is a plain REST API: no SDK required, and any language that can send an HTTP request can call it. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key, reducing adapter guesswork as a notebook-to-prod experiment becomes a service. These are integration advantages, not evidence about the quality of a device-risk model. Infrai also uses one key and one bill across backend services. That can reduce credential administration for a team integrating session controls with other backend capabilities, although it does not remove application authorization checks. Run a small inventory probe before wiring the button The implementation question asks for a Node.js account settings example. This walkthrough uses Python for the evaluation harness; the ownership rule and HTTP operations apply to the application server in either language. The smallest runnable probe lists sessions and prints the returned JSON without guessing response field names. Keep this server-side: a browser must never receive the service API key. Install the Python requests package in the harness environment, save the example as a Python file, and set INFRAI_API_KEY and VERIFIED_USER_ID. The latter must come from session verification for an isolated test account. It is a test-harness input, not an authentication mechanism for a production request. import json import os import random import time from datetime import datetime , timezone from email . utils import parsedate_to_datetime from urllib . parse import quote import requests def retry_delay ( value , attempt ) : if value : try : return max ( 0.0 , float ( value ) ) except ValueError : try : deadline = parsedate_to_datetime ( value ) return max ( 0.0 , ( deadline - datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) ) . total_seconds ( ) , ) except ( TypeError , ValueError , OverflowError ) : pass return ( 2 ** attempt ) + random . uniform ( 0.0 , 1.0 ) def list_sessions ( verified_user_id ) : user_id = quote ( verified_user_id , safe = "" ) for attempt in range ( 4 ) : response = requests . request ( method = "GET" , url = f "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/auth/session/list_for_user/{user_id}" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer " + os . environ [ "INFRAI_API_KEY" ] , "Accept" : "application/json" , } , timeout = 20 , ) if response . status_code == 429 and attempt < 3 : delay = retry_delay ( response . headers . get ( "Retry-After" ) , attempt ) response . close ( ) time . sleep ( delay ) continue if not 200 <= response . status_code < 300 : reason = response . text status = response . status_code response . close ( ) raise RuntimeError ( f "HTTP {status}: {reason}" ) try : return response . json ( ) finally : response . close ( ) raise RuntimeError ( "Retry budget exhausted" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : result = list_sessions ( os . environ [ "VERIFIED_USER_ID" ] ) print ( json . dumps ( result , indent = 2 ) ) Four attempts and a 20-second request timeout are example settings, not service limits or latency claims. The code honors Retry-After and otherwise uses exponential backoff with jitter. Add an overall deadline before putting the operation behind an interactive page. Run the probe privately; a shared notebook output is a poor home for a customer's session inventory. Next, build an adapter using the documented response schema. Normalize the session identifier, last-seen information, and a marker computed against the verified current session. These are application concepts, not asserted vendor JSON field names. The UI can then submit the selected identifier when a customer clicks revoke. Recheck ownership on that request, because a client can submit an identifier the page never displayed. Use the documented POST operation for individual session revocation. Generate one Idempotency-Key per logical write and reuse it on retries; don't generate a new key on every attempt. Record the actor, target, and operation identifier so interrupted requests can be reconciled with their audit records. The runnable read probe does not establish write correctness. Testing revocation requires exercising the selected credential after the operation, as well as refreshing the inventory. Evaluate recovery friction without moving the security boundary Start with explicit fixtures. Create two isolated customer accounts, with two sessions on the first account and one on the second. Mark one of the first customer's sessions as current and give the inventory records distinct last-seen times. Supply familiar-device and changed-fingerprint cases for each recovery path under evaluation. These are proposed inputs, not observed customer data or vendor response examples. Keep the fixture identities separate from real support tickets. The contract passes only if a body-supplied user ID cannot change the inventory, a foreign session cannot be revoked, and the current session receives explicit handling before the customer signs themselves out. Repeat delivery of one revoke operation must reconcile to one logical action with the actor recorded. Re-list, then try the revoked credential against a protected resource. A disappearing row alone is insufficient evidence of invalidation. Now test the scorer. Build a labeled evaluation set with legitimate recovery attempts and confirmed compromise cases, including customers who changed devices. Document how labels were established and hold out users from threshold tuning. Repeated sessions from the same customer should not leak across tuning and evaluation sets. For customer support, the primary decision is the recovery path: ordinary account controls, additional verification, or review under an established support policy. Fingerprint novelty is an input to that decision, not proof of theft. Set pass/fail criteria before looking at candidate results. A team might require zero successful cross-user actions in its adversarial fixtures and allow at most 5 extra verification prompts per 100 legitimate recovery attempts. Those are illustrative acceptance thresholds, not measured outcomes or universal security recommendations. Count missed compromise cases separately. Otherwise, a policy that never challenges anyone can appear attractive merely because it creates little friction. Compare a baseline without fingerprint-based escalation against the candidate on the same held-out inputs. Advance only if the authorization contract passes and the candidate meets the team's predeclared security and recovery-friction criteria. An empty count of misses in a tiny dataset does not establish a rare-event detection rate. Uncertain labels deserve review rather than quiet conversion into ground truth. Run Infrai as one measured leg through its adapter, recording contract outcomes and observed latency in the harness. No benchmark winner is assumed here. Session controls and risk scoring need separate results so successful HTTP calls cannot masquerade as evidence of detection quality. For a RAG or agent feature that explains a recovery decision, also evaluate explanation accuracy against the deterministic decision. Keep it out of enforcement. A prompt-cost aware experiment records input tokens, output tokens, and retries for that optional explanation, and compares its usefulness with a short deterministic message. Sending every device observation and the full session inventory into every prompt adds exposure and evaluation work before it proves any benefit. Compare providers by recovery ownership The useful comparison is who already owns the sessions and how precisely the required action maps to that authority. Put the same fixtures through each candidate adapter. Product documentation helps define the tests; it does not replace them. Candidate Concrete fit Recovery boundary to evaluate Infrai A backend wants per-user session inventory and individual revocation through plain REST, with inspectable schemas for its adapter. Keep device scoring in a separately evaluated component and verify the selected-session action end to end. Auth0 An application already using Auth0 should start with its documented session-management model. Map the required account-settings action to its session scope before adding another authority. Clerk An application using Clerk can evaluate its documented session controls within that integration. Test inventory, current-session presentation, and selected-session handling against the same fixtures. Supabase Auth A backend centered on Supabase Auth should inspect its documented session and sign-out semantics. Establish whether the required individual-session action matches those semantics; broad sign-out and selected-session revocation are different requirements. These products are not interchangeable merely because they all participate in authentication. Auth0's session-management documentation, Clerk's session documentation, and Supabase Auth's session guide describe different integration contexts. An existing identity provider that satisfies the recovery contract is the better choice than introducing another session authority and the reconciliation work that follows. For a team whose unresolved requirement is device-fraud detection, a specialist evaluated against labeled risk cases is a better next step than treating inventory as a detector. The trade-off is operational ownership. Plain HTTP keeps the Python harness independent of a vendor SDK, but the application still owns its adapter, authorization checks, UI safeguards, and recovery policy. Public schemas reduce field guessing; they do not decide what evidence support staff should accept. Move from notebook to production with an exit criterion Before release, confirm that request-time verification supplies the user identity, the page marks the current session, and a foreign target fails authorization. Exercise repeated clicks and interrupted revocations, then reconcile the operation with its actor record. Keep support access under its own authorization policy rather than borrowing a customer's settings flow. Review who can read the resulting telemetry and how long it stays available. Ship only after the contract tests and recovery-policy criteria both pass. Continue tracking unnecessary challenges and missed compromise cases separately, and rerun the held-out evaluation whenever fingerprint features or explanation prompts change. That keeps notebook-to-prod progress tied to a reproducible decision instead of a persuasive demo. Sources References for the security boundary and the competing session models: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet Auth0 session management Clerk sessions Supabase Auth sessions If this HTTP integration boundary fits your recovery workflow, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation .

title: WSGI vs ASGI, Uvicorn & Middleware: Explained from Absolute Zero 🚀
author: Deepika Pusala
summary: 🌱 WSGI vs ASGI, Uvicorn & Middleware: Let's Learn from ZERO! If you've built (or are building) a React + FastAPI project, you've probably run a command like this without thinking much about it: python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 But what actually happens when a request travels from your React frontend to your Python backend? 🤔 In this post, we'll learn step by step, with no prior knowledge required : ✅ WSGI vs ASGI ✅ Synchronous vs Asynchronous web servers ✅ The ASGI spec's minimal 3-callable interface ( scope , receive , send ) ✅ Uvicorn as an ASGI server ✅ ASGI middleware Let's go! 🎉 1. 🖼️ The Big Picture Imagine you open Instagram and click on a post. Behind the scenes: You click the post on the frontend (React) 🖱️ React sends an HTTP request to the backend The backend receives the request The backend processes it The backend sends a response React displays the post But here's the important question: ❓ Who actually receives the request and passes it to your backend application? That's where a web server comes in. 🍽️ Web server = the waiter in a restaurant Restaurant Web World 🧑 Customer Frontend (React) 🧑‍🍳 Waiter Web server (Uvicorn) 👨‍🍳 Kitchen Backend application (FastAPI) 🍕 Food Response The customer gives an order to the waiter, the waiter takes it to the kitchen, the kitchen prepares the food, and the waiter delivers it back. 📌 Important: FastAPI is your web application framework . Uvicorn is the web server that runs your FastAPI application. 2. 🕰️ What is WSGI? WSGI = W eb S erver G ateway I nterface. Don't get scared by the name! 😄 WSGI is simply a set of rules that answers one question: How should a Python web server talk to a Python web application? Think of two people, one speaking Telugu and the other Hindi. They need a common language to communicate. WSGI is that common language between a server and a Python app. 🔄 How WSGI works Client ──HTTP request──▶ WSGI Server ──WSGI rules──▶ Python App Client ◀──HTTP response── WSGI Server ◀────────────── Python App ⏳ Is WSGI synchronous? Yes, WSGI is fundamentally synchronous . Within a worker, the application handles one request at a time . Imagine 3 users, and each request takes 5 seconds : User Timeline What happens 👩 User A (profile) 0–5 s Processing A 👨 User B (feed) 5–10 s Waiting for A, then processing B 🧑 User C (notifications) 10–15 s Waiting for B, then processing C (Simplified: one worker, no parallel processing.) Examples of WSGI frameworks: Flask and traditional Django. 3. ⚡ What is ASGI? ASGI = A synchronous S erver G ateway I nterface. Like WSGI, ASGI defines rules for server ↔ application communication, but it supports something extra: asynchronous communication! It supports: 🌐 HTTP requests and responses 🔌 WebSockets ⏱️ Long-lived connections 🔁 Asynchronous operations 🔄 Same 3 users, now with async Each request waits ~5 seconds on a database: 👩 User A starts, then waits for the DB 👨 User B starts while A is waiting 🧑 User C starts while A and B are waiting The server keeps working on other requests while one is waiting. ✨ ⚠️ Important: ASGI doesn't automatically make everything async. Your application code and the libraries you use must support async behavior. 4. 🔀 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Remember these two lines: Synchronous = Wait until the current operation finishes before moving on. Asynchronous = Start an operation, and while it's waiting, work on something else. 🍜 Maggi analogy Sync: You put water to boil and stand there doing nothing until it boils. Then you add noodles. Async: You put water to boil, and while it boils , you chop vegetables. Waiting time = productive time! 🥕 📊 Technical difference Synchronous Asynchronous Blocking execution Can be non-blocking Waits for an operation Can do other work while waiting Usually normal functions Often uses async and await Less efficient for many I/O waits Handles many I/O waits efficiently 📥📤 What is I/O? I/O = Input/Output. Examples: Reading from a database 🗄️ Calling an external API 🌍 Reading a file 📄 Waiting for a network response 📡 🚨 One important distinction Async does NOT mean everything happens simultaneously. It means your program can switch to another task while one is waiting . Also: ❌ Async ≠ multithreading ❌ Async ≠ multiprocessing ❌ Async does not make CPU-heavy calculations faster 5. ⚔️ WSGI vs ASGI: Complete Comparison Feature WSGI ASGI Full form Web Server Gateway Interface Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface Execution Synchronous interface Asynchronous interface Communication Request and response Event-based communication HTTP ✅ Yes ✅ Yes WebSockets ❌ Not natively supported ✅ Supported Long-lived connections ❌ Not designed for them ✅ Supported Python callable Normal callable Async callable Example frameworks Flask (traditional) FastAPI, Starlette 💡 Clarification: WSGI does not mean a server can only process one user at a time. WSGI servers can use multiple workers, threads, or other concurrency techniques. Its limitation is the synchronous application interface , not an absolute inability to handle multiple requests. Similarly, ASGI doesn't mean every request runs simultaneously. It provides an asynchronous way to manage concurrent work . 💬 Why was ASGI introduced? Imagine building a chat app : User A: "Hi!" User B: "Hello!" User A: "How are you?" Messages can arrive at any time . A traditional request-response interface isn't naturally designed to keep a connection open and exchange many messages over time. ASGI supports WebSockets , which allow continuous two-way communication, and that's one of the biggest reasons it exists. 🎯 6. 🔑 The ASGI Spec's 3-Callable Interface You may have seen this code: async def application ( scope , receive , send ) : pass This is the basic structure of an ASGI application . The spec says an app must be an async callable that accepts exactly three arguments : scope receive send Let's understand each one. 👇 6.1 📋 What is scope ? Think of scope as an information sheet about the incoming connection. If React sends GET http://localhost:8000/feed , the server hands your app something like this: scope = { "type" : "http" , "method" : "GET" , "path" : "/feed" , "scheme" : "http" , "http_version" : "1.1" , } Key Meaning type What kind of connection? HTTP or WebSocket? method GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc. path Which URL path was requested? scheme HTTP or HTTPS? http_version Which HTTP version is used? 📝 Detail: For HTTP, the scope generally lasts for one request . For WebSockets, it lasts for the lifetime of the connection . 6.2 📥 What is receive ? When a user logs in, React might send: { "username" : "deepika" , "password" : "mypassword" } Your app needs a way to receive incoming messages from the server. That's receive : message = await receive ( ) receive() asks for the next incoming event await means wait until that event is available The event is stored in message An example message: { "type" : "http.request" , "body" : b '{"username": "deepika"}' , "more_body" : False , } (The b prefix means the body is bytes .) 📌 receive does not read directly from the internet. Uvicorn receives the network data and exposes it to your app through the ASGI receive channel. 6.3 📤 What is send ? Once your app has processed the request, it uses send to push the response out to the server: await send ( { "type" : "http.response.start" , "status" : 200 , "headers" : [ ( b "content-type" , b "text/plain" ) , ] , } ) This says: start an HTTP response, status 200, plain text. Then the body: await send ( { "type" : "http.response.body" , "body" : b "Login successful!" , } ) The server takes these events and builds the actual HTTP response for React. 🎁 🧩 Quick comparison Argument Question it answers Role scope What is this connection about? Method, URL, protocol, headers, etc. receive What is coming in ? Gets incoming events from the server send What should go out ? Sends outgoing events to the server 🧠 scope , receive , and send are not three separate servers. They are the three arguments the server gives to your ASGI app. 7. 🛠️ Let's Write Our Own Basic ASGI App! Create a file called main.py : async def app ( scope , receive , send ) : # Check the request type if scope [ "type" ] == "http" : # Send response status and headers await send ( { "type" : "http.response.start" , "status" : 200 , "headers" : [ ( b "content-type" , b "text/plain" ) , ] , } ) # Send response body await send ( { "type" : "http.response.body" , "body" : b "Hello Deepika!" , } ) Run it with: uvicorn main:app --reload What's happening? async def app(...) creates an async ASGI application scope holds request/connection info We check that the connection is HTTP We send the response status + headers We send the response body 🤯 Notice that we haven't used FastAPI anywhere! That's because ASGI is a specification, not a framework . FastAPI is simply a framework that follows this specification. 8. 🦄 What is Uvicorn? Let's connect everything: 📜 ASGI = the rules/specification 🧱 ASGI application = an app following those rules 🚪 Uvicorn = the server that runs the app Uvicorn is an ASGI web server. It receives HTTP requests from clients, talks to your ASGI app, and sends responses back. Think of it as the bridge between the outside world and your FastAPI app . 🌉 🔍 Breaking down the command python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 Part Meaning python -m Run a Python module uvicorn Start the Uvicorn server app.main Find main.py inside the app package :app Find the object named app inside that file --reload Auto-restart when code changes 🔁 --port 8000 Listen on port 8000 ⚙️ What happens when you run it? Uvicorn starts It imports your FastAPI application It starts listening on port 8000 React sends an HTTP request Uvicorn receives it Uvicorn converts the network request into ASGI information and events It calls your app with scope , receive , and send FastAPI processes the request FastAPI sends response events back Uvicorn converts those events into an HTTP response and sends it to React 📌 Uvicorn doesn't understand your business logic. It doesn't know how to log in a user, fetch a post, or check a password. That's your application's job. 🤔 Are Uvicorn and FastAPI the same? No! Uvicorn 🦄 FastAPI ⚡ Web server Web framework Receives network requests Defines API endpoints Implements ASGI server functionality Implements application logic Sends responses to clients Processes requests and creates responses from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI ( ) @app . get ( "/hello" ) async def hello ( ) : return { "message" : "Hello!" } FastAPI() creates your application app is your ASGI-compatible application object @app.get("/hello") defines an API endpoint uvicorn runs it ✨ You don't have to write scope , receive , and send manually. FastAPI and Starlette handle the ASGI communication internally. 9. 🛡️ What is ASGI Middleware? Middleware is code that runs between the web server and your main application . It can inspect, modify, or process incoming requests and outgoing responses. ✈️ Airport security analogy Before entering the airport: your identity is checked 🪪 → your luggage is scanned 🧳 → you pass security ✅ → you enter. Similarly, middleware performs checks before a request reaches your app. 🤷 Why do we need middleware? Instead of repeating the same logic in every endpoint, middleware can handle: 🔐 Authentication checks 🌍 CORS (allow/reject requests from particular origins) 📝 Logging incoming requests ⏱️ Measuring request time 🚨 Handling certain errors 🔒 Adding security headers 🔄 How middleware works Client → Middleware → Application Client ← Middleware ← Application Client sends a request Middleware receives it first Middleware performs its checks Middleware forwards the request to the actual app App processes the request Response comes back through middleware Middleware can inspect or modify the response Response reaches the client 🎯 Middleware works with both incoming requests and outgoing responses. 9.1 🐍 Raw ASGI middleware in Python class MyMiddleware : def __init__ ( self , app ) : self . app = app async def __call__ ( self , scope , receive , send ) : print ( "Request received!" ) await self . app ( scope , receive , send ) print ( "Response completed!" ) Line by line: Step 1: wrap the real app def __init__ ( self , app ) : self . app = app app is the actual application we want to wrap (e.g. your FastAPI app). We store it in self.app . Step 2: make it a valid ASGI callable async def __call__ ( self , scope , receive , send ) : Our middleware accepts the same three arguments as a normal ASGI app. Step 3: runs before the main app print ( "Request received!" ) Step 4: the most important line! 🌟 await self . app ( scope , receive , send ) This forwards the request to the actual application, as if saying: "Middleware is done. Now let FastAPI handle it." Step 5: runs after the inner app finishes print ( "Response completed!" ) 📝 This is a simplified ASGI middleware. Real middleware can also wrap receive and send to inspect or modify the messages themselves. 9.2 ⚡ Middleware in FastAPI (the easy way) You don't need to write low-level ASGI middleware every time: import time from fastapi import FastAPI , Request app = FastAPI ( ) @app . middleware ( "http" ) async def my_middleware ( request : Request , call_next ) : start = time . time ( ) response = await call_next ( request ) end = time . time ( ) print ( "Time taken:" , end - start ) return response @app.middleware("http") registers HTTP middleware request contains incoming request info call_next(request) passes the request to the next layer response stores the result We calculate the time taken return response sends it back 📌 This is a convenient FastAPI/Starlette interface, not the raw three-argument ASGI interface. For a GET /feed request, your terminal might show: Request received! Time taken: 0.035 seconds …and the user gets their feed. That's middleware! 🎉 10. 🧵 Putting It All Together in a React + FastAPI Project Here's the complete journey of a /feed request: 1. ⚛️ React frontend │ HTTP request: GET /feed ▼ 2. 🦄 Uvicorn (ASGI web server) │ Receives the network request, creates ASGI scope/receive/send ▼ 3. 🛡️ ASGI Middleware │ Logging, security, CORS, etc. ▼ 4. ⚡ FastAPI application (ASGI-compatible) │ Finds the /feed endpoint ▼ 5. 🗄️ Services / Repositories / PostgreSQL │ Business logic and data retrieval ▼ Response travels back up to React 🔙 11. 📚 Quick Terminology Cheat Sheet Term Simplest meaning Web server Receives network requests and sends responses Web framework Helps developers build backend applications WSGI Standard for synchronous Python server-app communication ASGI Standard for asynchronous Python server-app communication Synchronous Wait for an operation to finish Asynchronous Work on other tasks while an operation waits scope Information about an incoming connection receive Receives incoming event messages send Sends outgoing event messages Uvicorn An ASGI web server Middleware Code that wraps an app and processes requests/responses Event loop Coordinates and schedules asynchronous tasks Coroutine An async function that can pause and resume using await 12. 🧪 Test Your Understanding! Try these before looking at the answers. No stress! ❤️ What is ASGI? A) A Python database B) A communication standard between servers and applications C) A frontend framework Which one is the actual web server in a FastAPI project? A) React B) FastAPI C) Uvicorn What does scope contain? A) Connection/request information B) Database records C) Frontend CSS Which argument receives incoming ASGI messages? A) scope B) receive C) send What does middleware do? A) Stores images B) Wraps the application and processes requests/responses C) Replaces the database Does async mean everything happens simultaneously? A) Yes B) No 👀 Click to reveal answers B : ASGI is a communication standard between servers and applications C : Uvicorn is the web server A : Connection/request information B : receive B : Middleware wraps the app and processes requests/responses B : No, async means switching tasks while waiting, not running everything at once 13. 🎤 How to Explain This in an Interview WSGI and ASGI are standards that define communication between Python web servers and applications. WSGI follows a synchronous application interface, whereas ASGI supports asynchronous communication and protocols like HTTP and WebSockets. Uvicorn is an ASGI server that runs our FastAPI application. The ASGI application accepts three arguments: scope , receive and send . scope contains connection information, receive handles incoming events, and send handles outgoing events. Middleware sits around the application and can process incoming requests and outgoing responses before passing them along. 14. 🏁 Five Things to Remember Forever WSGI = Traditional synchronous application interface ASGI = Modern asynchronous application interface scope , receive , send = The three arguments of an ASGI app Uvicorn = The server that runs your FastAPI app Middleware = An extra layer that processes requests and responses 📖 Official Docs for Further Reading ASGI Introduction ASGI Specification Uvicorn: ASGI concepts Starlette Middleware 🚀 What's Next? The best way to make this stick: trace one real request through your own main.py → middleware → router → service → repository. Theory clicks when you see it in your own code! 💡 If this post helped you, drop a ❤️ or 🦄 and share it with a friend who's learning backend development. Happy coding! 👩‍💻✨

title: The chart was fine; the question it answered was wrong
author: LXSAIHUB
summary: I once put a time series in a pie chart. It was not a joke; I was in a hurry, the categories were months, and the result was twelve nearly identical slices that told nobody anything. The chart rendered. The config was valid. The question it answered was not the one anyone had asked. That is the part of data work that trips up engineers: we treat chart selection as a styling decision, when it is mostly a reasoning decision. Whether a column is categorical or temporal, whether you are comparing values, showing a distribution, or looking for a relationship, determines which chart type is even honest. Get that wrong and no amount of colour polish rescues it. Then there is the second, duller problem: even when you know the right chart, writing the config for your specific library is fiddly and different every time. Two problems I kept solving twice The first is the mapping from data shape to chart type. A time series wants a line, a part-to-whole comparison over categories wants bars, a distribution wants a histogram, a relationship wants a scatter. These are rules I know and still manage to get wrong at speed, especially when the data is pasted in as a raw block and I have not stopped to ask what the reader is supposed to conclude. The second is config drift. The same grouped bar chart is a different object in ECharts, Chart.js, and Recharts - different key names, different nesting, different defaults. I have lost more time to "why is the legend not showing" than to any statistical question. Remembering three option schemas is not a good use of a working memory that should be spent on the data. And then there is the sentence underneath the chart. A chart handed to an engineer and the same chart handed to a non-technical stakeholder need different captions. One wants the caveat about sample size; the other wants the one-line takeaway. Writing both is a small translation task nobody schedules. What I built I built ChartMind AI to take the raw block and do the boring middle. It reads your spreadsheet or numbers, recommends the best chart, writes the config for your library, and explains what the data actually means. The declared features are a best-chart recommendation, ready chart config per tool, plain-language insights, and audience-tuned output. That is the whole set. It does not run a statistical test, does not clean your data, and does not prove causality. The "ready chart config per tool" was the feature I wanted most. Getting a recommendation is nice; getting an option object I can paste into the library we actually use is the difference between a suggestion and a finished step. It removes the legend-key lookup that always broke my flow. The audience-tuned output is the quiet one. Asking for the insight in plain language, pitched at the person who will read it, is what stops a correct chart from being wrapped in a caption that either bores or overclaims. It is still a draft sentence, and I read it before it goes anywhere. The limits, stated plainly A chart recommendation is a heuristic over the data shape you paste, not a statistical analysis. It cannot tell you whether a trend is significant, whether a correlation is causal, or whether your sample is biased. The plain-language insights are descriptive text about the numbers, not findings, and they are only as good as the data you supplied - a messy column produces a confident sentence about messy data. None of this certifies your analysis; a person still has to stand behind the conclusion. I also want to be clear about the config. It targets the library you name, but libraries change and project setups differ; you still paste it in and check that it renders as intended. The tool does not execute your code or see your dashboard. If you have ever shipped a chart that rendered perfectly and answered the wrong question, ChartMind AI gives you a recommendation, a config, and a caption to start from. If a chart type you expected is missing, that is a gap and I would like to hear about it. FAQ What does ChartMind AI produce? A best-chart recommendation, a ready config for your charting library, plain-language insights, and output tuned to your audience. You paste the numbers into ChartMind AI and get the draft back. Does it prove the trend is statistically significant? No. It does not run statistical tests or establish causality. The insights are descriptive text, and a person still has to stand behind the conclusion. Will the config just work in my project? It targets the library you name, but setups and library versions differ. Paste it in and check that it renders as intended. Does it clean messy data for me? No. It works with the block you paste. A messy column in gives a messy read out.

title: Hitting 200 Strokes: What the Signature Maker Does at Its Stroke Limit
author: OnePassApps
summary: Hitting 200 Strokes: What the Signature Maker Does at Its Stroke Limit I work on OnePassApps, and this is our own app, measured on our own site. Our guide for the Signature Maker makes a promise we had never actually tested: "A signature holds up to 200 strokes and 40,000 points." Every post this account has written about that app so far quoted that line and moved on. This one is the test. What I measured, and where: the live app at app.onepassapps.com/apps/signature-maker, in one browser, one signed-out session, one build, on 11 November 2026. Every number below came out of that session. The counter is live. The panel counts strokes as you draw them and says so out loud: "1 stroke. Ctrl+Z undoes." Add strokes and it becomes "199 strokes. Ctrl+Z undoes." I started the pass with one long stroke already on the canvas, so the counter read one ahead of the strokes I was adding. The 201st stroke did not land. The app said: "This signature has reached its stroke limit. Undo a stroke or clear the canvas to keep drawing." That message appeared the first time I tried to add a stroke past the limit, and it stayed on screen. The counter then froze. It read exactly 200 for the next 20 strokes I tried to draw, fifteen in one pass and five in another. It never read 201, and the export size did not move either. Exporting still works at the ceiling. The export line kept reading "Exports at 1198 × 182 px, trimmed to the ink with a small margin." and the PNG at 2x downloaded as 52,090 bytes, measuring 1198 x 182 pixels. Reaching the limit stops drawing; it does not break the export. The other half of the guide's number, and where I got to. The guide also names 40,000 points. I dispatched 41,000 pointer-move events inside a single stroke. The app counted that as one stroke, never showed a point-limit message, and the vector export of that stroke held 3,999 curve commands - roughly 12,000 coordinate pairs - in 151,856 bytes, with viewBox "4 66 599 30", exactly one path element and no image tag. So whatever the app held internally, the SVG for that stroke was about 12,000 points, well short of 40,000. I am not claiming what happens at 40,000 points: I did not reach them, and I would rather say so than guess. Limits, stated plainly: one browser, one signed-out session, one build, one day, 11 November 2026. Strokes were driven with a mouse, so the pressure-aware width path, where a pen that reports pressure changes the line width, was not exercised. The counts are the app's own, read from its panel. The byte sizes are the downloaded files. The SVG figures are parsed out of the file itself. I did not use the Copy PNG button, I made no account, I uploaded nothing, and I changed nothing on the site. The guide, the app and the earlier post on this app are linked below. That earlier post measured the export formats in detail and left this ceiling untested; this post is the test it left open. title: JavaScript Deobfuscator Output: Reading It Layer by Layer
author: Devirt
summary: A JavaScript deobfuscator is a tool that rewrites obfuscated JavaScript into code a person can read: it decodes hidden strings, inlines helper functions, unwraps eval layers and straightens out tangled control flow. Most obfuscated scripts that land on an analyst's desk in November 2026, a card skimmer on a checkout page or a dropper in a phishing attachment, are built from the same four layers. Knowing those layers is what lets you judge whether the tool's output is the real logic or a confident guess. Where Devirt comes in: most obfuscated JavaScript gives way to the tools below. When a script turns out to be its own interpreter, running custom bytecode, Devirt handles the JavaScript VM deobfuscation and reports which recovered functions were proven, for code you own or are authorized to analyze. This post walks through the layers from the outside in, the way you meet them when you open a malicious script you've been asked to explain. It's written for defenders reading code found on their own or a client's systems. What does a JavaScript deobfuscator actually do? A JavaScript deobfuscator parses the script into a syntax tree (an AST), applies transformations that undo common obfuscation tricks, and prints the result as readable code. REstringer , for example, is built on an AST library, and synchrony runs AST visitors over the code. Working on the tree rather than on raw text is what lets a deobfuscator rename a variable everywhere it's used without breaking the script. They differ in which tricks they target. Some are tuned for output from javascript-obfuscator (the engine behind obfuscator.io), others handle older encoders such as Dean Edwards' packer or JSFuck, and picking between JavaScript deobfuscators mostly comes down to which technique each one undoes. This post is about the next step: reading what they hand back. One distinction first, because it comes up constantly: minification is not obfuscation. Minification shortens code so it loads faster, and a beautifier undoes most of it. Obfuscation changes code on purpose to make it hard to understand, and the same ideas behind code obfuscation in native programs (renaming, encoded strings, flattened control flow) show up in JavaScript as the layers below. Layer 1: the wrapper (eval, packers and encoders) The outermost layer of obfuscated JavaScript is usually a wrapper that builds the real code as a string and hands it to eval or the Function constructor. Dean Edwards' packer, JSFuck, AAencode and JJencode all produce wrappers like this. The visible script is a decoder; the program you care about only exists after it runs. Reading tip: the giveaway is a script whose last action is executing a string it just assembled. A deobfuscator unwraps this layer by evaluating the decoder in a controlled way and printing the string instead of running it. de4js and js-beautify both handle the classic packers this way. Layer 2: the string array Inside the wrapper, most modern obfuscated JavaScript moves every string literal into one large array, often shuffled, and replaces each use with a call to a small decoder function such as _0x3f2a(0x1b) . Function names, URLs and DOM selectors all disappear from view, which is the point: the strings are what tell you what a skimmer is after. Reading tip: find the array, then the function that indexes into it, then the short loop near the top that rotates the array before first use. Tools tuned for javascript-obfuscator output resolve this automatically. synchrony's README describes its string decoder as working with no configuration, and REstringer is built around reconstructing these strings. When this layer resolves cleanly, the script usually becomes legible. The strings name the targets. Layer 3: helper and proxy functions The third layer replaces simple operations with calls to tiny helper functions. a + b becomes _0x1c(a, b) , where _0x1c returns its two arguments added together. Comparisons, property lookups and calls get the same treatment, scattered across objects with meaningless keys. Reading tip: a deobfuscator inlines these proxy functions, replacing each call with the operation it wraps, then folds constants such as 0x4 * 0x2 + -0x8 down to a single value. If you're reading by hand, list each helper and what it returns before reading the main code. The main code reads very differently once you know _0x1c means + . Layer 4: flattened control flow and dead code The innermost layer breaks the order of the code. Control-flow flattening takes a function's statements, puts them in the cases of a switch inside an infinite loop, and drives the order with a counter or a string like "3|1|4|0|2" . Dead-code injection adds branches that can never run, to waste your time. Reading tip: follow the dispatch string and read the cases in that order, not top to bottom. A good JavaScript deobfuscator rebuilds the straight-line order and removes branches whose conditions are always false. Be careful with that second part, which leads into the next two sections. Is it safe to run a JavaScript deobfuscator on malicious code? Running a JavaScript deobfuscator on malicious code is only safe when nothing in the sample can execute outside a sandbox. Several of the layers above come off by evaluating part of the script, and evaluation is what the script's author wants you to do. REstringer's README says its unsafe modules run inside isolated-vm , and webcrack also depends on isolated-vm. That limits the damage, but it isn't a reason to paste a skimmer into an online playground. Analysts still run unknown scripts in an isolated lab, with no access to production networks, cookies or credentials, and keep the sample out of shared folders afterwards. How do you know the deobfuscated output is right? A JavaScript deobfuscator's output is trustworthy when it behaves the same as the original, and you can only claim that for what you checked. Three checks catch most errors: Strings: the decoded strings match what the original produces at runtime in your sandbox. A wrong rotation count gives plausible but wrong URLs. Behavior: the cleaned script makes the same network requests and DOM changes as the original when run on the same page in the lab. Removed branches: anything the tool deleted as "dead" can't run. Some branches only fire on a date, a domain or a fetched value, and a tool can misjudge them. Whatever you couldn't confirm, say so in the report. The labels Devirt uses for recovered code fit deobfuscated scripts too: proven, runtime-dependent (depends on data your sandbox didn't have), or unresolved. "We didn't see it exfiltrate anything" and "it can't exfiltrate anything" are different findings. When the code is an interpreter, not obfuscation Sometimes every layer comes off and the script still makes no sense. What's left is a loop that reads numbers out of a large array and calls one small function per number. That isn't obfuscated JavaScript any more. It's virtualized JavaScript: the protected functions were compiled into bytecode for an interpreter shipped inside the script. A JavaScript deobfuscator can tidy that interpreter, but it can't turn the bytecode back into the original functions, because the logic lives in the data, not in the code it rewrites. Some obfuscators also generate a new interpreter for every build, so the instruction set you work out for one sample doesn't carry over to the next. The difference between rewriting text and translating a virtual machine is the same one that separates devirtualization from deobfuscation in native binaries. At that point the job is JavaScript VM deobfuscation : working out what each handler does, mapping the opcodes, and lifting the bytecode back into readable logic, with a record of which functions were actually recovered. How to use a JavaScript deobfuscator, step by step Read obfuscated JavaScript from the outside in: unwrap, resolve strings, inline helpers, then reorder the flow. Let a deobfuscator do the mechanical work, then check its output against the original before you trust it. Stop when you hit an interpreter, because from there you're translating a virtual machine, not cleaning up code. If that happens on a script you're authorized to analyze, Devirt's free assessment tells you what can be recovered before anything is charged. Written by Devirt, an automated devirtualization service for authorized analysis of protected software.

title: We broke production with a one-word prompt edit and git could not tell us
author: LXSAIHUB
summary: The change was a single word. We softened "must" to "should" in a system prompt to make the tone friendlier. The agent stopped emitting one JSON field consistently, a downstream parser threw, and the incident review had no commit to point at - because the prompt did not live in the repo. It lived in a config row. That is the uncomfortable truth about a lot of agent code: the behaviour is defined by a prompt, and the prompt is treated like copy, not like code. It has no version history, no diff, no test, and no rollback. You can refactor a service all afternoon with guards around it, then ship a one-line prompt edit with nothing watching. The blast radius is the same. Why git-by-hand was not enough My first fix was to put the prompt in a .txt file and commit it. That bought us history and a rollback path, and it was worth doing. But a line diff on a long prompt is hard to read - a reworded paragraph shows up as a wall of changed lines - and, more importantly, a text diff says nothing about behaviour. Two prompts can differ in one word and behave completely differently on the same input. The thing I needed to test was not the text; it was what came out. The dangerous edit is the one that shifts a format or a refusal behaviour just enough that nothing throws and no one looks. So I kept a small fixed set of inputs that mattered to us, the ones whose output shape the rest of the system depends on. The check I wanted was simple: given the same inputs, does the edited prompt still produce the shape and constraints the old one did? That is a regression check, not a quality score. It does not say the new prompt is better, only that it did not silently break the cases we already rely on. What I built I built AgentPrompt to keep prompts under the same discipline as code. The declared features are version history, a diff view between any two versions, a regression check, and rollback. That is the whole set. It does not grade prompt quality, does not predict what a model vendor will change, and does not run your agent for you. The diff view is built for reading a prompt, not a source file: it shows you what changed between two saved versions so a one-word edit is visible as a one-word edit. Version history and rollback are the pair that make an experiment reversible. If a prompt change passes the checks and still feels wrong in practice, rolling back should be a click, not a reconstruction from a chat log. The regression check is the honest part. It covers the cases you give it. If you have not saved an input for a behaviour, the check has no opinion about that behaviour, and it should not pretend to. I would rather it report "no cases for this" than imply the prompt is safe. The limits, stated plainly A regression check over a fixed set of inputs cannot prove a prompt is correct, only that it has not broken the cases you recorded. Model behaviour can shift for reasons outside the prompt - a vendor update, a different temperature, a changed tool response - and this tool does not observe those. The diff is a text diff; it does not tell you two phrasings are semantically equivalent. None of this certifies a prompt or guarantees output. I also want to be clear about scope. AgentPrompt manages the prompt artifact itself. It does not replace integration tests for the rest of your system, and it is not a monitoring layer for live traffic. It is the version-and-check discipline that a config-row prompt was missing. If your agent's behaviour currently lives somewhere git cannot see, AgentPrompt gives you history, a readable diff, a regression check, and a way back. If a case you care about is not covered by your saved inputs, that is a gap in your set, not a false result. FAQ What does AgentPrompt do? It keeps version history, shows a diff between any two versions, runs a regression check, and lets you roll back. You manage the prompt in AgentPrompt instead of a config row. Does the regression check prove my prompt is correct? No. It only covers the input cases you saved. It cannot detect a behaviour you have no case for, and it does not grade quality. Will it catch a model vendor update breaking things? Not by itself. It checks the prompt against your recorded cases; it does not observe vendor changes, temperature, or tool responses. Is this a monitoring tool for live traffic? No. It manages the prompt artifact - history, diff, checks, rollback. It does not watch production requests.

title: I built a no-config way to host apps built in AI chats
author: Srujan Ranpise
summary: Woke up to 310+ installs on the Chrome Web Store, one month after launching Deployinn. Here's the story of why I built it. The problem AI chats are great at building apps. Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini can give you a working frontend, backend or full-stack project in a few minutes. Then you hit the part that isn't fun: Copy the code out of the chat Push it to a repo Pick a host and set up the project Wire up env vars Add a database Fix the build that breaks for some small reason For a personal project, that setup often took longer than writing the app. I got tired of it, so I built my own deployment platform. What Deployinn does Deployinn takes the code your AI builds and puts it live, with no config. There are three ways to use it: 1. Chrome extension. A deploy button appears inside the AI chat. Click it and the code goes live. 2. MCP connector. Add the connector link to your AI app, build something, and type "deploy this". 3. Agent CLI. For hands-free deploys from tools like Claude Code. A few things happen without extra setup: Your code is committed to your own GitHub A Postgres database is connected automatically when your app needs one The server scales up when traffic spikes It currently supports frontend, backend, full-stack and MCP server deploys. What I learned 1. The setup steps were the real problem. I thought the hard part would be hosting. It was actually the manual steps between "the AI wrote the code" and "it's live". 2. Meeting people where they already are matters. A deploy button inside the chat gets used more than a separate dashboard people have to remember to open. 3. Offering several entry points helps. Some people want a one-click button, some want to just ask the AI, and some want a CLI. I started with the extension and added MCP and the CLI later. 4. Early users find the edge cases quickly. The MCP connector and CLI are the newest parts, so they're the least battle-tested. Feedback on failed deploys has been the most useful input so far. Try it There's a free plan. title: Tobacco Stock & Backwoods: A Buyer's Guide to Classic Cigars

summary: Few cigar brands have earned a following as loyal as Backwoods . Since the first pack hit shelves, these slim, hand-finished cigars have become a familiar sight among smokers who want something simple, flavorful, and easy to enjoy. Their appeal is no mystery: a natural leaf wrapper, a slow and even burn, and a range of flavors that suit almost every taste. Unlike many mass-market cigars wrapped in uniform, machine-pressed sheets, they are finished in a natural tobacco leaf wrapper that gives each cigar a slightly different look and feel. That leaf carries real flavor, and it is a big reason the brand has stayed popular for decades. The cigars are also known for their size. They are slimmer and lighter than a traditional premium cigar, which makes them quicker to smoke and easier to carry. You get the character of a leaf-wrapped cigar without committing an hour to a single smoke. For many people, that balance of convenience and flavor is exactly the point. Another reason for their lasting popularity is consistency. Pack after pack, the burn stays steady and the taste stays true to the flavor on the label. A smooth, lightly sweet cigar that smells as good as it smokes. It is often the first pick for newcomers because the sweetness softens the natural tobacco taste. Sweet Aromatic. A dry cigar burns hot and tastes harsh, while a properly kept one stays smooth and flavorful from start to finish. title: Google's November Pixel Drop Brings Gemini Intelligence to Pixel 10 and Launches Pixel Tag
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: The November Pixel Drop is here, and it does what Pixel Drops do best: make older phones feel new again. Gemini Intelligence lands on Pixel 10, Call Screen gets smarter on Pixel 11, and Google is launching a brand-new gadget — Pixel Tag — on sale from November 11. Gemini Intelligence on Pixel 10 Gemini Intelligence is the headline. It gives Pixel 10 a smarter Gemini — more natural and expressive in conversation, with proactive suggestions and routines that follow your daily habits. One new piece is Rambler, which taps into your messages, emails and calendar to surface suggestions tied to the day ahead. Gemini Live can also handle multi-step tasks for you — Google's example is placing your morning coffee order. It's the phone doing the errands, not just answering questions. Call Screen gets an upgrade Pixel 11 owners get the other big phone change: Call Screen sounds more natural now, and it can check who is calling and why before you pick up. For the rest of the line, the Drop still brings plenty — the whole point of a Pixel Drop is that the phone you own gets better, not just the one Google wants to sell you. Pixel Tag, priced The surprise is hardware. Pixel Tag is Google's new tracker — a slim, keychain-ready tag for finding everyday items. It's available from November 11 at $29.99 for one, or $99.99 for a four-pack. Read the full announcement in Google's November Pixel Drop post . Pixel 10 owners get a smarter phone today; Pixel 11 owners get a better gatekeeper for their calls; and anyone prone to losing their keys can spend thirty bucks on insurance. Gemini has been busy lately — and Google's TPU chips are the hardware behind a lot of it. The Drop itself is free, as ever: it lands as a software update, and the only thing with a price tag is the Tag. Originally published on Rohan Tech Official .

title: Anthropic Launches Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and Meetings — Claude Becomes a Full Workspace
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: Claude is no longer just a chat window. Anthropic has launched Claude Sheets and Claude Whiteboards in beta on paid plans, made Claude Data generally available, shown off Claude Meetings for Team and Enterprise, and upgraded its interactive connectors. The pitch is plain: your whole working day, inside one app. Sheets and Whiteboards first The two headline additions arrive in beta on paid plans, across web, desktop and mobile. Claude Sheets brings spreadsheets into the conversation — ask Claude to build one and it will, formulas included. It has a 100,000-cell ceiling and 144 functions at launch, which is plenty for the models most people build day to day. Whiteboards, meanwhile, give Claude a shared surface to think on: drop ideas on a canvas, move them around, and watch the model work alongside you. Meetings, with a caveat Claude Meetings is the one to read carefully. Anthropic showed it off for Team and Enterprise customers, with Google Meet support at launch — Claude joins the call, takes notes and updates documents live as the meeting runs. It's still in beta, though, and the framing is "coming soon" rather than fully live. The idea is clear enough: the meeting notes write themselves, and the follow-up document is already half done by the time the call ends. The connectors get bigger The other piece is connectivity. Interactive connectors now let apps like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, Notion and HubSpot open in full beside a Claude conversation, so the work — and the context — never leaves the window. Anthropic says more than 9,000 plugins are now listed in the Claude Marketplace. Read the full announcements on Anthropic's news page or head to Claude to try the new tools. Anthropic has been shipping fast lately — Claude Fable 5.2 landed just days ago, and the contest with OpenAI's Businesses in ChatGPT is now a head-on race.
