title: Meituan Releases LongCat-2.5 — A 1.6-Trillion-Parameter Open-Weight Model Under the MIT License
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: Another trillion-parameter model just went open weight — and this one's licence is about as permissive as they come. Meituan has released LongCat-2.5, a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 1.6 trillion parameters in total and around 48 billion active on each token, under the MIT license. Anyone can use it, change it and build on it, including for commercial work. What LongCat-2.5 is built for LongCat-2.5 is aimed squarely at agents. Meituan describes it as a native multimodal mixture-of-experts model built for long-horizon agent tasks — the kind of work where a model has to keep going for a long stretch, pulling in different kinds of input along the way. It builds on the earlier LongCat-2.0, and the company says it marks a first step toward systems that can handle "superhuman-scale" agent work. The sparse design is the trick: most of the model's 1.6 trillion parameters stay dormant on any given token, with only about 48 billion switching on. What the MIT licence changes Plenty of open-weight models come with strings attached — custom licences that limit commercial use or demand a revenue share. An MIT licence carries none of that. Builders can fine-tune LongCat-2.5, ship it in a product and charge for it without asking Meituan first. Meituan's announcement points to the model on Hugging Face , where the weights, config and licence are all listed. The parameter count, in context Is 1.6 trillion parameters a lot? Yes — but the number that matters for anyone running the model is the 48 billion active per token. That's the slice that actually does the work, so running costs land closer to a much smaller model. Sparse models like this one are common now, and the race is over who can squeeze the most ability out of each active parameter. Google's new TPU 8tx chips are built for exactly this kind of agentic AI — and the same week saw DeepMind's AI formally verify Signal's crypto protocol . The models are getting bigger, the proofs are getting harder, and the licences are getting looser. Whether LongCat-2.5 finds its way into real products is the test that counts — and with an MIT licence, there's nothing stopping anyone from trying. Originally published on Rohan Tech Official .

title: OpenAI Launches Businesses in ChatGPT in Beta — Business Hub and AI Agents for Every Storefront
author: Rohan Tech official
summary: ChatGPT is starting to look a lot like a search engine — and OpenAI knows it. The company has launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a way to claim their profile, keep their product information current in a new Business Hub, and run AI agents that talk to customers on their behalf. For now, the Business Agents are open to eligible ecommerce and online-service businesses in the US. What businesses actually get The Business Hub is the control panel: claim your business, manage product info, and see aggregated insights about how people find you. From there, a Business Agent can hold conversations with customers — answering questions, recommending products, and pointing people toward a purchase. OpenAI's announcement , published on November 10, frames it as a way for businesses of every size to put a storefront inside the app where millions of people already ask questions. The company also says ads in ChatGPT will give businesses a new way to reach customers. Why this looks familiar TechCrunch put it bluntly, saying OpenAI is making ChatGPT "just a little bit more like Google" — a place where businesses manage a profile, show up in answers, and pay to be seen. Search has worked that way for years; the difference here is that the storefront is a conversation. Shoppers don't type a query and pick a link — they ask a question, and the agent answers as if it works for the shop. What it means for storefronts For a small business, the pitch is hard to ignore: a customer-facing agent that never sleeps, inside an app your customers already open every day. The open question is whether shoppers will actually buy through a chat — and whether businesses trust an AI to speak for them. OpenAI has been aiming its models at security work too, building AI models built for security , and the same logic applies here: an agent that talks to your customers has to be one you can trust with your brand. As AI moves into everyday products — even formal verification of crypto protocols is now AI's work — the storefront may be the next place it feels normal. Either way, ChatGPT's role is shifting. It's not just a place to ask questions any more — it's a place where businesses show up to answer them. Originally published on Rohan Tech Official .
